questions.stem: In international law, the word 'states' usually refers to:
options: non-government groups that campaign for human rights
independent countries with a government and territory
the six Australian states that make up the federation
international organisations such as the United Nations
questions.explanation: In international law a state is a sovereign country with a defined territory, a population and a government. International organisations and NGOs take part in international law, but they are not states, and Australia's states have no standing to make treaties.

questions.stem: Sovereignty, in international law, is best described as:
options: the duty of every state to ratify the main human rights treaties
a state's supreme authority over its own territory and people
the power of the United Nations to make laws binding on all countries
a monarch's personal right to rule without the consent of parliament
questions.explanation: Sovereignty means a state has supreme authority within its own borders and is not subject to any higher law-maker. This is why treaties bind a state only if it consents to them; the United Nations has no general power to legislate for countries.

questions.stem: Australia and New Zealand sign an agreement on extradition between the two countries. This treaty is best described as:
options: multilateral, because it is made between two states
a covenant, because it sets out civil and political rights
a declaration, because it is not binding on either state
bilateral, because it is made between two states
questions.explanation: A bilateral treaty is made between two states, while a multilateral treaty has many parties, such as the ICCPR. Treaties of either kind bind the parties; a declaration such as the UDHR is not itself a treaty.

questions.stem: Which statement about the terms 'treaty', 'convention' and 'covenant' is correct?
options: A covenant is binding only on states that drafted it at the United Nations
A convention is an agreement between a state and its own citizens
All three describe binding written agreements between states
Only a treaty binds states; conventions and covenants are guidelines
questions.explanation: Convention and covenant are names for treaties, and each binds the states that become parties to it. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the Convention on the Rights of the Child are both binding treaties despite their different titles.

questions.stem: A country's foreign minister signs a new human rights treaty, but the country does not yet ratify it. What is the main legal effect of signing?
options: The treaty automatically becomes part of the country's domestic law
The country may later join only by accession, not by ratification
It shows an intention to be bound and a duty not to defeat the treaty's purpose
The country is fully bound by every obligation in the treaty from the day of signing
questions.explanation: Signature generally signals an intention to become bound and an obligation not to undermine the treaty's object and purpose, but the state is not bound by its terms until it ratifies. Ratification, not signature, is the act by which a state consents to be bound.

questions.stem: A state that did not sign a treaty when it was open for signature later agrees to be bound by it. This process is called:
options: reservation
derogation
accession
ratification
questions.explanation: Accession is how a state becomes a party to a treaty it did not sign; it has the same legal effect as ratification. Australia acceded to the 1951 Refugee Convention and to the First Optional Protocol to the ICCPR. Ratification follows an earlier signature.

questions.stem: When it ratified the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women in 1983, Australia stated that it was not then in a position to introduce paid maternity leave throughout Australia. This statement is an example of:
options: an optional protocol, which adds a complaints process to the treaty
an accession, which joins a treaty that the state did not sign
a reservation, which excludes or modifies a treaty obligation for that state
a derogation, which suspends all the treaty's obligations during an emergency
questions.explanation: A reservation is a statement made when joining a treaty that excludes or modifies the legal effect of certain provisions for that state. A reservation cannot be incompatible with the treaty's object and purpose. A derogation is a temporary suspension of some rights during a public emergency.

questions.stem: A bill of rights is best described as:
options: a treaty that sets out the rights of states in their dealings with each other
a list of the law-making powers given to the Commonwealth Parliament
a report by the United Nations on a country's human rights record
a document that sets out the basic rights of people within a country
questions.explanation: A bill of rights lists the fundamental rights of people in a country, either entrenched in a constitution or passed as an ordinary Act. Australia has no national bill of rights; Queensland, Victoria and the ACT have statutory human rights Acts.

questions.stem: The International Bill of Human Rights consists of:
options: the UDHR, the UN Charter and the Geneva Conventions
the ICCPR, the CRC and the Refugee Convention
Magna Carta, the UDHR and the ICCPR
the UDHR, the ICCPR and the ICESCR
questions.explanation: The International Bill of Human Rights is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) and the two 1966 covenants: the ICCPR and the ICESCR. The UN Charter and the Geneva Conventions are important instruments, but they are not part of it.

questions.stem: The right to a fair trial, the right to vote and freedom of expression are protected mainly by the:
options: International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights
Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities
Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees
International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
questions.explanation: Civil and political rights, such as a fair trial, voting, expression and freedom from arbitrary detention, are in the ICCPR. The ICESCR covers rights such as work, social security, health and education.

questions.stem: The ICESCR requires each state to take steps 'to the maximum of its available resources' to achieve its rights progressively. Which right is this principle most likely to apply to?
options: The right not to be subjected to torture
The right to freedom of thought and religion
The right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty
The right to the highest attainable standard of health
questions.explanation: Progressive realisation applies to economic, social and cultural rights, such as health and education, which need resources to be achieved over time. Freedom from torture and the presumption of innocence are civil and political rights that states must respect immediately.

questions.stem: Australian H V Evatt is associated with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights because he:
options: refused, on Australia's behalf, to vote for the declaration
presided over the General Assembly when it adopted the declaration
wrote the declaration alone at the request of the Security Council
was the first person to bring a complaint under the declaration
questions.explanation: Dr H V Evatt, Australia's Minister for External Affairs, was President of the General Assembly session that adopted the UDHR on 10 December 1948. The declaration was drafted by a commission chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, and it has no complaints process of its own.

questions.stem: The 1967 Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees was significant because it:
options: created the UN High Commissioner for Refugees to protect refugees
required every state to resettle a fixed number of refugees each year
removed the 1951 Convention's time and geographic limits
added environmental disasters as a ground for gaining refugee status
questions.explanation: The 1951 Convention originally applied to people who became refugees because of events before 1 January 1951, and states could limit it to events in Europe. The 1967 Protocol removed those limits so the definition applied worldwide. UNHCR was created by the General Assembly in 1950.

questions.stem: Under the Refugee Convention, the principle of non-refoulement means that a state must not:
options: hold an asylum seeker in detention while their claim is assessed
allow a refugee to apply for citizenship until ten years have passed
return a refugee to a place where their life or freedom is at risk
refuse entry to any person who arrives at its border without a visa
questions.explanation: Non-refoulement, in article 33 of the Refugee Convention, forbids returning a refugee to a place where they would face persecution on a Convention ground. The Convention does not require states to admit everyone without a visa, and it does not set a citizenship waiting period.

questions.stem: The International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD) is implemented in Australian law mainly by the:
options: Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld)
Migration Act 1958 (Cth)
Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth)
Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth)
questions.explanation: The Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth) was passed to give effect to ICERD, which Australia ratified in 1975. The Sex Discrimination Act 1984 implements CEDAW.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) is correct?
options: It is a non-binding declaration adopted by the General Assembly in 1948
It applies only to women who are refugees or asylum seekers
It requires states to end discrimination against women in public and private life
It protects women only from discrimination by governments, not by employers
questions.explanation: CEDAW (1979) is a binding treaty that requires states to take all appropriate measures to eliminate discrimination against women, including by private persons and organisations. Australia gave effect to it through the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth).

questions.stem: Article 2 of the Convention against Torture states that no exceptional circumstances, such as war or a public emergency, may be used to justify torture. This means the prohibition is:
options: temporary, so it lapses during an armed conflict
absolute, so it cannot be limited or suspended
progressive, so it is achieved as resources allow
optional, so it applies only if a state accepts it
questions.explanation: The prohibition of torture is absolute: no war, threat of war or emergency can justify it, and an order from a superior is not a defence. Many other rights can be reasonably limited, but not this one.

questions.stem: Under the Convention on the Rights of the Child, a child is generally a person:
options: under 14 years of age
under 21 years of age
under 18 years of age
under 16 years of age
questions.explanation: Article 1 of the CRC defines a child as every human being below 18, unless majority is reached earlier under the law that applies to the child. The CRC is the most widely ratified human rights treaty.

questions.stem: A Queensland agency must decide whether a child's family should be reunited in Australia. Under article 3 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, what must be a primary consideration?
options: The wishes of the child's eldest relative
The cost of the decision to the government
The views of the child's school principal
The best interests of the child
questions.explanation: Article 3 of the CRC requires that in all actions concerning children, the best interests of the child be a primary consideration. The child's own views must also be given weight according to age and maturity under article 12.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) is to:
options: create new rights that only people with disability can claim against the state
provide guidelines on disability services that states may choose to follow
allow states to make separate laws for people with disability in institutions
ensure people with disability enjoy all human rights equally with others
questions.explanation: Article 1 of the CRPD states its purpose as promoting, protecting and ensuring the full and equal enjoyment of all human rights by persons with disabilities. It mainly applies existing rights to people with disability rather than creating separate rights, and it is binding on parties such as Australia.

questions.stem: Australia has ratified a treaty but the Commonwealth Parliament has not passed any law to implement it. A person tries to enforce a right in the treaty in an Australian court. The most likely result is that:
options: the court cannot directly enforce the treaty, because it is not part of domestic law
the court must enforce the treaty, because ratification makes it binding domestic law
the court must refer the case to the International Court of Justice to decide
the court must declare any Australian law inconsistent with the treaty invalid
questions.explanation: In Australia, ratified treaties do not become part of domestic law until parliament passes legislation implementing them. Courts may use a treaty to help interpret ambiguous legislation, but they cannot enforce it directly or strike down laws for being inconsistent with it.

questions.stem: In Minister for Immigration v Teoh (1995), the High Court held that Australia's ratification of the Convention on the Rights of the Child gave rise to a legitimate expectation that decision-makers would act consistently with it. What is the best explanation of this case's importance?
options: It showed that the High Court can declare Commonwealth laws contrary to a treaty invalid
It showed that an unincorporated treaty could still affect government decision-making
It showed that the Convention had become part of domestic law on ratification
It showed that parents could take their complaints directly to the United Nations
questions.explanation: Teoh found that ratification alone could create a legitimate expectation that officials would treat the best interests of the child as a primary consideration, or give the person a chance to respond. The Court did not say the Convention was domestic law, and it cannot invalidate laws for breaching a treaty.

questions.stem: The Human Rights (Parliamentary Scrutiny) Act 2011 (Cth) requires a member who introduces a bill into the Commonwealth Parliament to:
options: prepare a statement of compatibility with human rights for the bill
obtain the approval of the Australian Human Rights Commission
show that the bill complies with every treaty Australia has signed
refer the bill to the High Court for an opinion on its validity
questions.explanation: Section 8 requires a statement of compatibility assessing whether the bill is compatible with human rights. The Act also set up the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights to examine bills, Acts and legislative instruments.

questions.stem: Under the Human Rights (Parliamentary Scrutiny) Act 2011 (Cth), 'human rights' means the rights recognised in:
options: the express and implied rights found in the Australian Constitution
the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the common law
the human rights Acts of Queensland, Victoria and the Australian Capital Territory
seven core international human rights treaties, including the ICCPR and the CRC
questions.explanation: Section 3 defines human rights by reference to seven treaties: the ICERD, ICESCR, ICCPR, CEDAW, CAT, CRC and CRPD, as they apply to Australia. The UDHR is not a treaty and is not in the list.

questions.stem: A bill passes both houses of the Commonwealth Parliament even though its statement of compatibility admits that it limits the right to liberty. Which statement best describes the legal position?
options: The Act cannot commence until the joint committee approves the limitation
The Act must be read down by courts so that it does not limit liberty
The Act is valid, because the statement does not bind courts or affect validity
The Act is invalid, because the statement shows it breaches a ratified treaty
questions.explanation: Section 8 states that a statement of compatibility is not binding on any court or tribunal and that failure to comply does not affect the validity of the Act. The scrutiny model informs parliament but leaves it free to pass laws that limit rights.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest criticism of the Human Rights (Parliamentary Scrutiny) Act 2011 (Cth) as a protection of human rights?
options: It requires every bill to be approved at a referendum when rights are affected
It applies only to Queensland bills, so most Commonwealth laws are unaffected
Its reports cannot stop a bill passing, so a government majority can ignore them
It lets the High Court strike down laws that the joint committee finds incompatible
questions.explanation: The Act improves transparency and debate, but the committee's reports are advisory and bills can pass before it reports. It gives no power to courts to invalidate laws, and it applies to Commonwealth bills and instruments, not state laws.

questions.stem: Article 2(1) of the United Nations Charter is based on the principle of:
options: the duty to intervene to protect civilians
the sovereign equality of all its members
the veto of the five permanent members
the universal right to seek asylum
questions.explanation: Article 2(1) states that the UN is based on the principle of the sovereign equality of all its members, so each state is legally equal regardless of size or power. The veto belongs to the Security Council's procedures, not to this principle.

questions.stem: State A sends troops across its border to seize part of State B's territory. Which article of the UN Charter has State A most clearly breached?
options: Article 2(7), which bars the UN from intervening in matters within domestic jurisdiction
Article 2(1), which makes the UN responsible for defending every member's borders
Article 2(4), which allows force only when the General Assembly approves it
Article 2(4), which bans the threat or use of force against a state's territorial integrity
questions.explanation: Article 2(4) requires members to refrain from the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state. The Charter's exceptions are self-defence and action authorised by the Security Council, not the General Assembly.

questions.stem: A government accused of abusing a minority group tells the UN that the matter is purely internal and that the UN has no right to interfere. Which article of the UN Charter is it relying on?
options: Article 2(7), which forbids any criticism of a state by other states
Article 2(7), on matters essentially within a state's domestic jurisdiction
Article 2(4), on the use of force against a state's territorial integrity
Article 2(1), on the duty of members to protect human rights everywhere
questions.explanation: Article 2(7) says nothing in the Charter authorises the UN to intervene in matters essentially within the domestic jurisdiction of a state, except for Security Council enforcement measures under Chapter VII. States often cite it against outside scrutiny, which creates tension with the universality of human rights.

questions.stem: The main role of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) is to:
options: protect refugees and stateless people and help find lasting solutions for them
prosecute leaders who force people to flee their homes during armed conflicts
decide disputes between states about the return of refugees to their homelands
issue passports that allow refugees to travel to any member state of the UN
questions.explanation: UNHCR, established by the General Assembly in 1950, leads international action to protect refugees and stateless people and supports voluntary return, local integration and resettlement. It cooperates with states in applying the Refugee Convention. Prosecutions happen in courts such as the ICC.

questions.stem: Magna Carta, sealed by King John in 1215, is important to human rights because it:
options: listed universal human rights that later became the Universal Declaration
placed the monarch under the law and promised free men lawful judgment
gave every adult in England the right to vote for members of a new parliament
abolished the monarchy in England and replaced it with an elected president
questions.explanation: Magna Carta established that the king was subject to the law and promised that no free man would be imprisoned or punished except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land. These ideas underpin the rule of law, due process and trial by jury. It did not create voting rights.

questions.stem: A Queensland real estate agent refuses to rent a unit to a couple because of their national origin. Under which Commonwealth Act could they make a complaint?
options: Age Discrimination Act 2004
Disability Discrimination Act 1992
Racial Discrimination Act 1975
Sex Discrimination Act 1984
questions.explanation: The Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth) makes discrimination on the basis of race, colour, descent or national or ethnic origin unlawful, including in housing. The complaint would go first to the Australian Human Rights Commission.

questions.stem: Section 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth) makes it unlawful to:
options: employ a person of one racial background in preference to a better applicant
refuse to hire an applicant because of their political opinions
do a public act likely to offend, insult or humiliate a person because of race
hold a private belief that one racial group is superior to another
questions.explanation: Section 18C makes racially offensive public acts unlawful, and it is a civil wrong rather than a crime. Section 18D exempts acts done reasonably and in good faith, such as fair reporting and genuine academic or artistic work.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) is correct?
options: It creates a criminal offence punishable by imprisonment for any discrimination
It allows employers to dismiss a worker who becomes pregnant without notice
It prohibits sexual harassment and requires employers to take steps to prevent it
It applies only to discrimination against women in Commonwealth workplaces
questions.explanation: The Act, which gives effect to CEDAW, prohibits discrimination on grounds such as sex, pregnancy and family responsibilities and makes sexual harassment unlawful. Employers now have a positive duty to take reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate sexual harassment. It protects people of any sex in most areas of public life.

questions.stem: A restaurant refuses to serve a customer who uses an assistance dog. Which Act is most relevant to her complaint?
options: Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth)
Disability Discrimination Act 1992 (Cth)
Age Discrimination Act 2004 (Cth)
Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth)
questions.explanation: The Disability Discrimination Act 1992 makes it unlawful to discriminate against a person with disability in areas such as providing goods and services, including because they use an assistance animal. It defines disability broadly to include physical, intellectual, psychiatric, sensory and other conditions.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old applicant is told he will not be interviewed because the employer wants 'young energy', while a 19-year-old is refused a lease because the landlord thinks young people are unreliable. Which statement about the Age Discrimination Act 2004 (Cth) is correct?
options: It cannot apply to either, because age is protected only by state law
It can apply to both, because it protects people of all ages
It can apply only to the older applicant, because it protects people over 55
It can apply only to the young applicant, because employment is excluded
questions.explanation: The Age Discrimination Act protects people of any age from unlawful discrimination in areas such as employment and accommodation, subject to listed exemptions. It is not limited to older people, although many complaints concern older workers.

questions.stem: In Koowarta v Bjelke-Petersen (1982), the High Court held that the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth) was valid. On which head of power did the Act rely?
options: The corporations power in section 51(xx), as it regulated businesses
Section 109, as it gave Commonwealth laws priority over state laws
The external affairs power in section 51(xxix), as it implemented ICERD
The race power in section 51(xxvi), as it applied to people of all races
questions.explanation: The Court held that the Commonwealth could rely on the external affairs power to pass laws implementing a treaty it had ratified, here ICERD. Section 109 is not a head of power; it decides which law prevails when valid laws conflict.

questions.stem: In 1985 Queensland passed a law declaring that any traditional land rights in the Murray Islands had been extinguished without compensation. In Mabo v Queensland (No 1) (1988) the High Court held the law invalid. Why?
options: It was made under a residual power that Queensland had given to the Commonwealth
It was inconsistent with the ICCPR, which Queensland courts must enforce directly
It was inconsistent with section 10 of the Racial Discrimination Act (section 109)
It breached section 116 of the Constitution, which protects the free exercise of religion
questions.explanation: Section 10 of the Racial Discrimination Act guarantees equality before the law regardless of race, and the Queensland law removed rights only from the Islanders. Because the state law was inconsistent with a valid Commonwealth law, section 109 made it invalid. Courts do not enforce the ICCPR directly.

questions.stem: A student argues that Australians' rights are fully protected because the Commonwealth can implement every treaty using the external affairs power. Which is the strongest counter-argument?
options: The power applies only to treaties signed before Federation in 1901
The High Court has held that the power cannot be used to protect human rights
Laws made under the power can be overridden by any inconsistent state law
The power allows protection but does not require it, and such laws can be amended
questions.explanation: The external affairs power lets parliament implement treaties, but whether it does so is a political choice, and statutes such as the Racial Discrimination Act can be amended or suspended by later Acts. Section 109 means valid Commonwealth laws prevail over inconsistent state laws, not the reverse.
